clue.text: Hospital department quick to bandage injury

indicators.note: a bandage is wound right round the thing it covers, so the word here closes over the letters beside it

parts.note: pacy means quick, as in a pacy thriller; it opens up to take the insertion
harm is injury done to someone

explanation.surface: A hospital department that is swift to dress a wound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quick' looks like praise for the department's service and is really the four letters doing the wrapping. Pacy is ordinary British usage for anything that moves at speed.
explanation.definitionFit: The pharmacy is the hospital's dispensary, the department that makes up and hands out the drugs.

clue.text: Malty hop puzzled expert crossing fields

indicators.note: someone puzzled is mixed up, so the letters of these two words are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A brewer is baffled by a hop with a malty taste.
explanation.walkthrough: 'puzzled' tells you to rearrange the eight letters of MALTY HOP; the definition is the cryptic-sounding 'expert crossing fields'.
explanation.definitionFit: A polymath is a person of wide learning whose expertise spans many different disciplines.

clue.text: Creativity without which our world would be what?

indicators.note: the clue asks what our world would be with something removed, so the answer's letters are taken away from the world word

parts.note: our world is the planet Earth
eh is an exclamation asking someone to repeat themselves, like 'what?'

explanation.surface: A rhetorical question about how empty life would be without creativity.
explanation.walkthrough: Take ART out of EARTH and you are left with EH, which is 'what?' as a query, so the clue's joke-question has a literal answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Art is the expression of human imagination and skill, so creativity names it fairly.

clue.text: Spooner's rude manner, a somewhat dotty way to communicate

definitions.text: a somewhat dotty way to communicate

indicators.note: Spooner's says to swap the opening sounds of the two words, as the Reverend Spooner famously did

parts.note: coarse means rude or vulgar
a mode is a manner or way of doing something

explanation.surface: A tongue-tangled cleric's rude manner, described as a rather silly way to get a message across.
explanation.walkthrough: Rude manner is COARSE (said as CORSE) MODE; 'Spooner's' swaps the first sounds, as the Reverend Spooner would. 'dotty' is a pun: the code is made of dots and dashes.
explanation.definitionFit: Morse code sends messages as dots and dashes, so it is quite literally a dotty means of communication.

clue.text: City club maybe opening in Islington with volume right up

indicators.note: a club is only one of the four suits, so 'maybe' warns that an example is standing in for the general word

parts.note: a club is a playing card, one of the four suits

indicators.note: the opening of a word is the letter it starts with

parts.note: the opening letter of Islington
ff is fortissimo on a score, the marking that tells a player to be very loud

explanation.surface: A London nightclub launching with the music turned up loud.
explanation.walkthrough: Islington is an inner London borough, which keeps the surface firmly in the wrong city while handing over one letter of a Welsh one. Fortissimo's ff is the loudest ordinary dynamic a composer writes.
explanation.definitionFit: Cardiff is the capital of Wales, so the bare word 'City' names it by category.

clue.text: Tricky opening golf range

parts.note: golf is G in the radio alphabet
an ambit is the range or scope a thing covers, as in the ambit of a law

explanation.surface: An awkward first shot down at the golf range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tricky opening' sounds like the hard first hole of a course, and golf is on hand to encourage that. A gambit is a chess opening that concedes a pawn to win position.
explanation.definitionFit: A gambit gives something away early to gain the advantage, so it is an opening with a trick in it.

clue.text: Chain with eyelets at both ends

parts.note: and joins two things the way 'with' does

indicators.note: the letters standing at both ends of a word are the two on its outside

parts.note: the outer letters of EYELETS

explanation.surface: A length of chain finished with an eyelet at either end.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface assembles a piece of hardware and 'chain' reads as the metal sort; the answer is a mountain chain. 'Eyelets' is not wanted for its meaning at all, only for its first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Andes run the whole length of South America, and a range of mountains strung out like that is a chain.

clue.text: Boys initially distribute exam, one marked before new term?

indicators.note: an initial is the letter a word starts with, so only the front of this word is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of Boys
to allot is to distribute in shares
the paper is the exam itself, as in sitting three papers

explanation.surface: Boys handing round an exam that somebody marked before term began.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Term' is a school term on the surface and a term of office in the answer, and the marking is a cross in a box rather than a teacher's red pen.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballot paper is the sheet a voter marks with a cross, after which the winner takes up a new term in office.

clue.text: Tiresome noise from unhappy baby changing sides in cot

indicators.note: the two sides of the word cot are its outer letters; changing sides swaps the one for the other

parts.note: crying is the noise an unhappy baby makes

explanation.surface: A wailing baby in its cot, turning from one side to the other, is exhausting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changing sides in cot' means swapping the letter on one side of COT (C) for the one on the other (T), done here to the noise of an unhappy baby.
explanation.definitionFit: Trying means testing one's patience, wearisome, the same as tiresome.

clue.text: Force has ceremonial kit covering uniform

indicators.note: a cover lies over a thing on both sides, so the word goes round what it covers

parts.note: ceremonial dress is the kit worn on parade
uniform is U in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: A police force turned out in its parade uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uniform' is the radio alphabet's U, not the outfit the surface has everybody wearing. Duress is force of the coercive kind — a confession signed under duress.
explanation.definitionFit: Duress is pressure brought to bear to make someone act against their will, which is force in the sense of compulsion.

clue.text: Tesla cracks concrete after flipping further down the road

indicators.note: one thing cracking another breaks into it, so the Tesla letter goes inside the other piece
flipping turns the word for concrete back to front

parts.note: concrete as an adjective means real, actual
T is the SI symbol for the tesla, the unit of magnetic flux density

explanation.surface: An electric car crashes into a concrete barrier after overturning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tesla' looks like the car maker but gives T, the symbol for the scientific unit. 'after flipping' turns REAL into LAER, and 'cracks' puts T inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something further down the road happens at a subsequent time, an idiom for afterwards.

clue.text: Trot across circle then pause in circular dance

indicators.note: to go across a thing is to span it from one side to the other, ending up on both sides of it

parts.note: to trot is to run at an easy pace
O is the letter drawn as a circle
a delay is a pause in proceedings

explanation.surface: A horse trotting across the ring and then stopping.
explanation.walkthrough: A roundelay is an old song with a refrain that comes round again, and the ring dance performed to it. 'Trot' reads as the horse's gait while supplying a plain word for running.
explanation.definitionFit: A roundelay is danced in a ring, the dancers going round as the refrain comes round.

clue.text: Attract wrinkly men? It's age

indicators.note: wrinkly suggests something creased and rumpled, so the letters of the words after it are jumbled

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether older men are attractive, and the answer is that it's age that does it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrinkly' seems to describe the men, but it is the signal to rearrange MEN ITS AGE.
explanation.definitionFit: To magnetise is to draw something or someone towards you, as a magnet pulls iron.

clue.text: Powerful car adjusted, muting roars

indicators.note: something adjusted has been altered and rearranged, so these letters change order

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A high-performance car has been modified to silence its engine noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adjusted' tells you to rearrange the eleven letters of MUTING ROARS.
explanation.definitionFit: A gran turismo is a high-performance touring vehicle built for speed over long distances.

clue.text: Tin-filling method demonstrated

indicators.note: what fills a thing sits inside it rather than beside it

parts.note: Sn is tin's symbol in the periodic table, taken from the Latin stannum
the how of a thing is the method of doing it

explanation.surface: A tin-filling technique being put through its paces.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen makes 'Tin-filling' look like one compound adjective, which buries the instruction inside it. Tin's chemical symbol is nothing like its English name because it comes from stannum.
explanation.definitionFit: A method that has been shown has been demonstrated — the same past participle either way.

clue.text: Criticise dyke builder's mistake after rupture

indicators.note: what comes after a thing is placed behind it, so the piece named second in the clue is reached first in the answer

parts.note: a tear is a rupture in cloth
Offa, king of Mercia, threw up Offa's Dyke along the Welsh border in the eighth century
a trip is a stumble, and so a slip or mistake

explanation.surface: A dyke builder blamed for a blunder once the wall gave way.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe moves and Offa's trip becomes off a strip. Offa's Dyke is the earthwork the Mercian king raised along the Welsh border, and long stretches of it are still walkable.
explanation.definitionFit: To tear someone off a strip is to give them a dressing-down, British for a sharp spoken rebuke.

clue.text: As usual, king enjoying Cambs town's amenities?

parts.note: R is rex, Latin for king, the letter that follows a monarch's name
anyone making the most of what the place has to offer is OUT IN ELY; Ely is the small cathedral city in Cambridgeshire

explanation.surface: A king having a good night out in a small cathedral city.
explanation.walkthrough: Cambs is the everyday shortening of Cambridgeshire on signs and addresses. The long phrase about amenities has to be reread as a place you are standing in before it gives up any letters.
explanation.definitionFit: What is done routinely is done as usual, as a matter of course, and both work as adverbs.

clue.text: Religious campaigner's vintage blue clothes for Easter

parts.note: a cru is a named growth or vineyard, the word a French label uses for a wine's pedigree
feeling blue is feeling sad

indicators.note: clothes go round the outside of what they cover, so what is wanted is the letters on the outside

parts.note: the outer letters of EASTER

explanation.surface: A gloomy campaigner in the old blue outfit he keeps for Easter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothes' is the setter's favourite word for a container and is doing something else here — taking the outermost letters rather than putting anything inside. Cru turns up on wine labels as premier cru and grand cru.
explanation.definitionFit: The Crusaders marched on the Holy Land under the cross, so a crusader is a campaigner with religion behind the campaign.

clue.text: Superficially thuggish crook steals superior Renaissance painting

indicators.note: superficially means on the surface only, so just the outside letters of thuggish
crook as a verb means bend out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: upper means higher or superior

explanation.surface: A thug only on the surface, a criminal pinches a fine Renaissance artwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crook' looks like a noun for the thief but bends STEALS into ELASTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonardo da Vinci's mural of Christ's final meal is a famous work of the Italian High Renaissance.

clue.text: Like bog Bill is on

indicators.note: in a down answer what is on something rests above it, so this piece goes on top

parts.note: a bill is a poster, and what a poster carries is an ad
a mire is boggy ground

explanation.surface: A poster pasted up over a patch of marsh.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital on 'Bill' makes it a man standing in the bog, and it is a printed bill instead. Down clues let 'on' mean directly above, which settles the order.
explanation.definitionFit: To admire someone is to think highly of them, the same warm approval as liking them, and both are verbs.

clue.text: Harass soldiers repeatedly, time after time

parts.note: T is the standard abbreviation for time
OR is Other Ranks, the British army's soldiers below officer rank
the instruction to take soldiers a second time, now as plain men
time again, and this one brings up the rear

explanation.surface: Soldiers being pestered over and over, day after day.
explanation.walkthrough: Two different words for soldiers are wanted rather than the same one twice: the army's Other Ranks first, then simply men. 'Time after time' reads as an adverb and is a T at each end.
explanation.definitionFit: To torment someone is to keep on at them until it hurts, which is harassing them.

clue.text: Total that is under 100 — someone helping with your golf?

indicators.note: in a down answer what is under something sits below it, so these letters go beneath

parts.note: C is a hundred in Roman numerals
to total a column of figures is to add it up
i.e. is short for id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A sum that comes to less than a hundred.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash is where the clue turns: arithmetic before it, a golf course after. 'Under' has to be read as position in the grid rather than as size.
explanation.definitionFit: A caddie carries a golfer's clubs round the course and advises on the shot, which is help of a hands-on kind.

clue.text: Chambers occupied with circulating what lungs take in

indicators.note: what circulates goes round and comes back the other way, so these letters run backwards

parts.note: lungs take in air, set down backwards
someone hard at a job is occupied with it

explanation.surface: Rooms busy with air being moved around them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chambers' sits comfortably in the surface, since rooms are chambers too, and the ones meant are inside the heart. Blood really does circulate through them, which keeps the misdirection medical throughout.
explanation.definitionFit: The atria are the two upper chambers of the heart, where blood arrives before being pumped on.

clue.text: E in solo transposed up a third throughout

indicators.note: in music, a note transposed up a third moves two letter names up the scale

parts.note: alone means solo, by oneself
the letter E, read as the musical note

explanation.surface: Musical directions: a note in a solo passage is shifted up a third, all the way through.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is musical: 'transposed up a third' moves the note E two letter names up the scale to G (E, F, G), and that change is made in the word for solo.
explanation.definitionFit: Along can mean all the way through, as in 'all along', which is the sense of throughout.

clue.text: Appreciate artist cutting chocolate bar for eating festival

indicators.note: to cut into a thing is to open it up and go inside it

parts.note: a Mars bar is the chocolate bar, opened up to take the insertion
to dig something, in the old slang sense, is to appreciate it
RA is a Royal Academician, the crossword's standard artist

explanation.surface: An artist cutting up a chocolate bar to enjoy at a food festival.
explanation.walkthrough: Two pieces go into the Mars bar together, which is what disguises where the bar is split. 'Dig' for appreciate is 1960s slang that crosswords have kept in service.
explanation.definitionFit: Mardi Gras is Fat Tuesday, the day of feasting that uses up the rich food before Lent's fasting starts.

clue.text: Detective scrubs face for evening speech

parts.note: DI is a Detective Inspector
scours means scrubs clean

indicators.note: the face of a word is its front, so its first letter

parts.note: its first letter is used

explanation.surface: A police detective washes their face before going out for the evening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scrubs face' reads as one action but splits: scrubs is one piece, and 'face for' takes the front letter of evening. DI is the British police abbreviation for Detective Inspector.
explanation.definitionFit: A discourse is a formal spoken or written treatment of a subject, a speech.

clue.text: Two people checking story admit government stole

indicators.note: two of them are called for, so the same piece is taken twice, one on either side
to admit someone is to let them in, so the letter goes inside

parts.note: the person who checks a story before it runs is the editor, ED
G is the standard abbreviation for government

explanation.surface: A pair of sub-editors verifying a story that involves the government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stole' is the past tense of steal in the sense of moving quietly — he stole out of the room — not of theft, and the newsroom surface works hard to keep you on the theft.
explanation.definitionFit: To edge towards a door is to get there a little at a time without drawing attention, which is how someone steals out.

clue.text: Quit with rude gesture for boss

parts.note: to go is to quit a place
the V-sign, two fingers raised with the palm turned inwards, is the British insult, and the letter is the shape it makes

explanation.surface: Walking out of a job with a two-fingered farewell to the manager.
explanation.walkthrough: The V-sign is Britain's own rude gesture, distinct from the single finger, and it is the letter it draws that the clue wants. Gov, short for governor, is how a London cabbie or workman addresses whoever is in charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Gov is the everyday British address for the man in charge, clipped from governor.

clue.text: Zip shortened on back of costume as much as required

indicators.note: in an across clue on means placed after, so the zip piece follows the costume letter
the back of a word is its last letter
shortened means cut off at the end, so the zip word loses its final letter

parts.note: zip is slang for nothing, nought

explanation.surface: A dressmaker shortens the zip at the back of an outfit to just the right length.
explanation.definitionFit: Enough means a sufficient quantity, exactly what is needed.

clue.text: Toes vary wildly, accept hosts at bedtime

indicators.note: wildly means in an uncontrolled, disordered way, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: People's feet differ enormously in shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wildly' signals an anagram of TOES VARY; the definition is the playful phrase about accepting hosts at bedtime.
explanation.definitionFit: To stay over is to spend the night at someone else's home as their guest.
